 ## Search results
The closest match is [HSTU-BLaIR (KDD workshop, 2025)](https://kdd2025llm4ecommerce.github.io/assets/accepted/13_HSTU_BLaIR_Lightweight_Cont.pdf): projected text embeddings enrich item-ID embeddings before HSTU sequence encoding, with sampled-softmax next-item training. This supports integrating content inside one HSTU network. However, its fixed 125M-parameter BLaIR encoder uses external Amazon-review pretraining, so its text pipeline is ineligible here; “lightweight” does not mean trained from scratch. [Original HSTU (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152) supplies the compatible sequential backbone, rather than a demonstrated scratch-trained title/description encoder.

A constraint-compatible hypothesis, inferred from that fusion design: randomly initialized token embeddings, separate masked pooling of title and description, then a small projection and learned residual gate into item-ID embeddings. Share the resulting item representation between history encoding and candidate scoring; jointly optimize all parameters through the HSTU next-item loss. A shallow CNN could preserve local phrases and model-number distinctions that mean pooling loses. These are proposed adaptations, not established findings from the retrieved papers. Search did not identify a directly matching 2024–2026 study demonstrating lightweight, scratch-trained title/description encoding jointly with HSTU. Keep content limited to observed metadata; compatibility should emerge from ordered training interactions, without inferred attributes, review signals, external weights, or separately fitted scores.

---

Meta’s 2024 HSTU reference configuration uses sampled softmax with 128 negatives, temperature 0.05, and L2-normalized item/user representations—useful objective choices to test while retaining the HSTU backbone. These MovieLens settings are a starting point, not evidence of optimality on the four Amazon categories. [Official configuration](https://github.com/meta-recsys/generative-recommenders/blob/main/configs/ml-1m/hstu-sampled-softmax-n128-final.gin). RecSys 2025’s *Correcting the LogQ Correction* shows that in-batch sampling disproportionately penalizes popular items; its refined correction accounts for the positive being always present rather than sampled. Sampling correction must match the actual proposal distribution; applying ordinary logQ correction blindly to mined negatives is unjustified. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331).

Practical hypothesis: compare uniform multi-negative sampled softmax against a mixture of uniform and moderately hard negatives scored by the same HSTU, gradually increasing hardness and excluding observed training positives. Treat this as an experiment: false negatives can represent real interests, so selecting only the highest-scoring unseen items risks suppressing relevant recommendations. [False-negative research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116). More negatives also compete with batch size: a 2026 preprint reports advantages from larger batches under its fixed batch-times-negatives memory budget, rather than universally maximizing negative count. [Preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11061). The supplied Electronics statistic—10.71% of negatives outranking positives—motivates investigation but does not establish its cause. Select experiments using the unchanged macro validation HR@10, with one trained HSTU checkpoint per category; larger training margins alone do not establish ranking generalization.

---

HSTU already provides a natural temporal extension point: learned relative position/time biases inside its SiLU attention, followed by multiplicative gating of aggregated values. These mechanisms can learn temporal relevance without replacing the causal backbone. The original paper supports this architecture, but does not establish that recency alone distinguishes persistent preference from completed purchase intent. [HSTU, 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.17152v3). A 2025 generative-ranking paper also retains temporal information while investigating cheaper alternatives to quadratic relative biases, highlighting their computational cost. [Towards Large-scale Generative Ranking](https://genai-personalization.github.io/assets/papers/GenAIRecP2025/9_Huang.pdf).

Purchase-cycle research suggests avoiding a single monotonic decay: MgRIA reports repeated-purchase intervals combining a power-law trend with weekly/monthly periodic spikes. These findings concern repurchase tasks; transfer to unseen-item recommendation remains uncertain. [MgRIA, 2026](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1567422326000037). More directly, SAM models post-purchase satiation through time-sensitive suppression/recovery gates and a time-to-next-purchase auxiliary objective. Its mechanism depends on click/purchase distinctions and repeat histories that this benchmark may not supply. [Learning to Forget, 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12714).

Experiment hypothesis: retain one jointly trained HSTU per category; add bucketed elapsed-time attention biases and a small internal gate conditioned on observed inter-event gaps and causal hidden states. Let the gate modulate recent versus broader historical information, without imposing universal decay or claiming observed purchase completion.
